title: The trial of the created Qur'an
word: The trial of the created Qur'an
hook: a question of theology becomes a test given by the state, and one scholar won't give the answer

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mu'tazilah, who stressed justice and oneness, and said the Qur'an was created.

Questions of theology usually live in books and lecture halls. You can disagree about them over dinner and still pass the bread. But for a stretch of the Abbasid caliphate, one question went to court. Judges and scholars were called in and asked, one by one: is the Qur'an created? There was a right answer, and the government had chosen it. Some said the words and went home. Some would not, and among them was a scholar in Baghdad, Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
screen: `A QUESTION GOES TO COURT.` → `IS THE QUR'AN CREATED?` → `ONE SCHOLAR WON'T SAY IT.`

segments.voice: The episode has a name in Arabic: al-mihna, the trial, or the ordeal. It began with the caliph al-Ma'mun, who took up the Mu'tazili view that the Qur'an was created and ordered officials to test the scholars on it. Those who refused could lose their posts, or worse, and the policy outlived him, carrying on under the caliphs after him. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, whose name the Hanbali school carries, kept refusing. The accounts of his life, collected by his family and students, say he was held in chains, questioned, and beaten. And they give his answer again and again, in one shape: show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. They also show what he did not do. He didn't call for a revolt, raise an army, or curse the caliph from the pulpit. He just wouldn't say the sentence. Some reports say that afterward he forgave the men who had him beaten. In time a later caliph, al-Mutawakkil, ended the policy. Two things came out of it. In Sunni theology, Ibn Hanbal's position, that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, became the standard one. And the scholars took a lesson about who settles questions of belief. A ruler had tried, with prisons and whips, and it hadn't worked. The state stepped in, and the state stepped back out. What stayed was a quiet man who kept asking for a verse.
screen: `AL-MIHNA: THE TRIAL.` · `A CALIPH CHOOSES THE ANSWER.` · `SHOW ME A VERSE.` · then, large: `THE STATE STEPPED BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little straighter, the way you might in a hard meeting, and bring to mind one thing you hold to, something you'd quietly decline to say even if it made life easier. Notice your jaw and hands, and let the shoulders drop while you keep the conviction: firmness doesn't need clenching. If you pray, ask in your own words for steadiness; if not, just keep the posture, back straight, shoulders soft.
The trial of the created Qur'an. Al-mihna: when caliphs enforced the Mu'tazili view, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused to give the answer. Today's word.
screen: `THE TRIAL OF THE CREATED QUR'AN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the state stepped in. And a quiet scholar outlasted it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the mihna as the time caliphs tried to enforce the doctrine of the created Qur'an, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal is honored, especially among Sunnis, for refusing under pressure.

chat.says: Did Ahmad ibn Hanbal lead a revolt against the caliph during the trial?
options: No. He just refused to say it, and kept asking for a verse or sunnah.
Yes. He raised an army in Baghdad until the caliph backed down.
Yes. He cursed the caliph from the pulpit every single Friday.
chat.meaning: The accounts say he didn't revolt or curse the caliph. He wouldn't say the sentence, and asked for proof from the Book or the sunnah.

al-mihna.meaning: the trial or ordeal: testing scholars on the created Qur'an

al-Ma'mun.meaning: the Abbasid caliph who began the test

Ahmad ibn Hanbal.meaning: Baghdad scholar who refused; the Hanbali school carries his name

al-Mutawakkil.meaning: the later caliph who ended the policy

sunnah.meaning: the Prophet's way: his words and practice

sources.ref: Accounts of the mihna of Ahmad ibn Hanbal (e.g. Salih ibn Ahmad, Sirat al-Imam Ahmad; Hanbal ibn Ishaq, Dhikr mihnat al-Imam Ahmad)
sources.work: Early biographies of Ahmad ibn Hanbal

sources.ref: al-Tabari, Tarikh, on al-Ma'mun's letters ordering the test

notes: No dates given deliberately. Confirm the sequence: begun under al-Ma'mun, continued under his successors, ended by al-Mutawakkil.
'Held in chains, questioned, and beaten' and 'some reports say he later forgave those who had him beaten': confirm against the early biographies.
'Show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah' is a paraphrase of his reported reply, not a quotation.
'Became the standard position in Sunni theology': confirm wording; Twelver Shia and Ibadi views on the createdness of the Qur'an differ and are not discussed here.
